entry.gloss: three or more notes sounded together
entry.def: Three or more different notes sounded together. In common-practice music most chords are built from thirds stacked above a root, starting with the triad.

entry.gloss: three-note chord built of stacked thirds
entry.def: A chord of three notes: a root, the third above it and the fifth above it. Stacked as closely as possible in root position, its notes lie on three neighboring lines or three neighboring spaces.

figure.staff: [C4 E4 G4]/h [D4 F4 A4]/h [G4 B4 D5]/h
figure.caption: Triads on lines and on spaces.

entry.gloss: the note a chord is built on and named after
entry.def: The note on which a chord is built by stacking thirds, and after which it is named: C is the root of a C major triad, whichever of its notes is lowest.

entry.gloss: chord note a third above the root
entry.def: The note of a chord a third above its root: E in a C major triad and Eb in a C minor triad. Whether this third is major or minor decides whether a triad sounds major or minor.

entry.gloss: chord note a fifth above the root
entry.def: The note of a chord a fifth above its root: G in a C major triad. In major and minor triads it is a perfect fifth, in diminished triads a diminished fifth and in augmented triads an augmented fifth.

entry.gloss: the root is the lowest note
entry.def: A chord is in root position when its root is the lowest note, whatever the order of the notes above it.

entry.gloss: the third of the chord is the lowest note
entry.def: A triad is in first inversion when its third is the lowest note. In figured bass and Roman numeral analysis it is marked 6, short for 6/3, from the sixth between the lowest note and the root.

entry.gloss: the fifth of the chord is the lowest note
entry.def: A triad is in second inversion when its fifth is the lowest note. It is marked 6/4, from the sixth and fourth above the lowest note.

entry.gloss: major third and perfect fifth above the root
entry.def: A triad with a major third and a perfect fifth above its root, so a minor third lies on top of the major third: C–E–G.

entry.gloss: minor third and perfect fifth above the root
entry.def: A triad with a minor third and a perfect fifth above its root, so a major third lies on top of the minor third: C–Eb–G or A–C–E.

entry.gloss: minor third and diminished fifth above the root
entry.def: A triad of two stacked minor thirds, with a minor third and a diminished fifth above its root: C–Eb–Gb, or B–D–F, the triad on the seventh degree of C major. Written with a small circle, as in vii°.

entry.gloss: major third and augmented fifth above the root
entry.def: A triad of two stacked major thirds, with a major third and an augmented fifth above its root: C–E–G#. It is the triad on the third degree of the harmonic minor scale, and is written with a plus sign, as in III+.

entry.gloss: the notes of a chord played one after another
entry.def: The notes of a chord played one after another instead of together, from the Italian word for playing the harp. Also called a broken chord.

figure.staff: C4/e E4/e G4/e C5/e E5/e C5/e G4/e E4/e | C4/w |.

entry.gloss: chord label: the scale degree of its root
entry.def: A label that names a chord by the scale degree of its root: I for the triad on the tonic, V for the triad on the dominant. Upper case marks a major triad, lower case a minor triad, lower case with ° a diminished triad and upper case with + an augmented triad.

figure.staff: [C4 E4 G4]/q{I} [D4 F4 A4]/q{ii} [E4 G4 B4]/q{iii} [F4 A4 C5]/q{IV} [G4 B4 D5]/q{V} [A4 C5 E5]/q{vi} [B4 D5 F5]/q{vii°} [C5 E5 G5]/q{I}
figure.caption: The triads of C major.

entry.gloss: a note's numbered place in the scale
entry.def: The position of a note in a scale, counted from the tonic as 1. Each degree has a number, often written with a caret above it, and a name such as dominant.

entry.gloss: first degree: the home note of the key
entry.def: The first degree of a scale, which names the key and where melodies and harmonies come to rest. The triad built on it, I or i, is the tonic triad.

entry.gloss: second degree: a step above the tonic
entry.def: The second degree of a scale, a step above the tonic.

figure.staff: C4 *D4{2} E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5

entry.gloss: third degree: midway from tonic to dominant
entry.def: The third degree of a scale, midway between the tonic and the dominant. Whether it lies a major or a minor third above the tonic tells major from minor.

figure.staff: C4 D4 *E4{3} F4 G4 A4 B4 C5

entry.gloss: fourth degree: a fifth below the tonic
entry.def: The fourth degree of a scale. Its name means the lower dominant: it lies a fifth below the tonic, as the dominant lies a fifth above.

figure.staff: C4 D4 E4 *F4{4} G4 A4 B4 C5

entry.gloss: fifth degree: a fifth above the tonic
entry.def: The fifth degree of a scale, a perfect fifth above the tonic. After the tonic it is the most important degree: the dominant triad, V, leads strongly back to the tonic.

figure.staff: C4 D4 E4 F4 *G4{5} A4 B4 C5

entry.gloss: sixth degree: a third below the tonic
entry.def: The sixth degree of a scale. Its name means the lower mediant: it lies a third below the tonic, midway between the tonic and the subdominant below it. In a major key it is the tonic of the relative minor.

figure.staff: C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 *A4{6} B4 C5

entry.gloss: seventh degree a half step below the tonic
entry.def: The seventh degree when it lies a half step below the tonic, so that it leads up to it. In minor keys it is the raised seventh degree, as in the harmonic minor scale. Called the leading note in British English.

figure.staff: C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 *B4{7} C5

entry.gloss: seventh degree a whole step below the tonic
entry.def: The seventh degree when it lies a whole step below the tonic, as in the natural minor scale. Some books use the word for the seventh degree in general.

figure.staff: A4 B4 C5 D5 E5 F5 *G5{7} A5
figure.caption: In A natural minor, G is the subtonic; raised to G# it becomes the leading tone.
